title: Each returns to its root
hookLine: reach utmost emptiness, hold to stillness; all things return to their root (Tao Te Ching 16)
carry: returning to the root is stillness

lines: A CUP, A BREATH, AN EMPTY HUB, MUDDY WATER.
cards: Lay this week's chapters side by side and that's the direction they keep pointing: a cup not filled to the brim, a soft breath like a sleeping baby's, the hole in a wheel's hub, too many colors and a numb eye, praise and blame both startling, something you look for and can't see, a jar of muddy water set down to clear.
Chapter sixteen of the Tao Te Ching, today's chapter, names where that direction leads. It calls it the root.

teach.h: EMPTINESS AS FAR AS IT GOES.
teach.b: First, the instruction. The chapter opens by asking for emptiness taken as far as it goes, and stillness held steadily. Not a picture this time, but something close to a method: empty out, and keep still.
Second, what you see from there.
From that stillness, you watch all things rise and watch them return. Things grow and flourish, and each goes back to its root. A leaf comes out in spring and falls in autumn.
A thought appears and fades. A wave lifts and sinks back into the sea. The rising is real.
So is the going back. Third, the chain. Then a short ladder.

teach.h: THE ROOT IS STILLNESS. CLEAR SEEING.
teach.b: Returning to the root is stillness. Stillness is going back to what you're meant to be. That is the constant.
Knowing the constant is called clear seeing. Not knowing it, the chapter warns, people act blindly and bring trouble on themselves. Each step leans on the one before, so it's worth reading slowly.
Fourth, comfort as well as teaching. Whoever knows the constant, the chapter ends, becomes open, and from openness comes fairness, and so on, step by step, up to the Tao, which lasts.
To the end of one's life, it says, there is no danger. Some readers hear reassurance as much as instruction. Things go back where they came from.
You don't have to drag yourself there. You return.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter sixteen as a guide to sitting still: they watch thoughts and sensations rise and fall away, and keep coming back to the quiet beneath them.

games.q: what does “return to the root” mean?
o: everything rising, then going back to stillness
going back to the village where you were born
digging up a plant to check that it's healthy

games.q: this week's chapters: tap the pairs.
p: let the muddy water be still

s: chapter sixteen says returning to the root is stillness
and stillness is going back to what you're meant to be.
the chapter says only living things return to their root
it says all things rise and return; each goes back to its root.
the chapter says not knowing the constant is harmless
it warns that people who don't know it act blindly and bring trouble on themselves.

games.q: you're sitting still and a thought rises. chapter sixteen says you watch things rise. what comes next?
o: follow the thought to see where it goes.
watch it go back down, returning to its root.
push it away as fast as possible.
games.why: the chapter says all things rise, and each returns to its root. you watch the rising and the going back.

practice: Let the breath be soft, the way it was on the first day of this week, and watch what rises: a sound, a thought, an itch, a memory. Don't follow it out; watch it come up and sink back, the way a wave returns to the sea.
Each time you notice you've wandered, that noticing is the return, so come back to the stillness and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Return to the root. Chapter sixteen's picture: everything that rises goes back where it came from, and that going back is stillness. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: return to the root, the phrase at the center of chapter sixteen.

carryVoice: Your line: returning to the root is stillness. Whatever rises goes back where it came from. Until tomorrow.
